newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Oil futures deflate as reality sets in.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil futures deflate as reality sets in.

text.p: Something akin to the rapid deflation in U.S. share prices may be rearing its head in the oil world, as futures prices on Wednesday plunged to their lowest level in more than a year.
Traders of physical oil were not so much surprised by the sharp sell-off in oil futures in New York and London than by how long it has taken for the real supply-demand situation to filter through.

"I really can't believe it has taken this long for crude prices to come down," said one broker in Houston, Texas. "Look, there has never been a time in the past few months that you couldn't find crude."

Crude futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) ended Wednesday at their lowest level since early March last year, pressured by figures from the Department of Engery showing growing oil imports and rising domestic inventory.
Benchmark NYMEX oil futures for May delivery settled down 81 cents at $19.47 a barrel.
NYMEX futures had tumbled more than 25 percent since the start of the year to late-February but then climbed again to peak two weeks ago at $22.65.

For weeks, bearish players in the cash market have trumpeted oversupply scenarios, saying prices for U.S. belwether West Texas Intermediate, delivered at Cushing, Texas, at more than $22.00 a barrel were ludicrous.

"There never was a bull market in crude. When the world's largest marginal producer is holding back, keeping crude off the market, then it is not a bull market," said Bill O'Grady, oil analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis, Mo, referring to Saudi Arabia, which is pumping at a rate of about eight million barrels a day, or about two million barrels below capacity.
"You also have to throw in OPEC cheating, which happens most often when the dollar is strong," O'Grady added.
Cash crude dealers said the move into "contango" in the oil markt was a harginger of things to come.
Contango occurs when the nearby futures contract, currently May crude, is valued below the second month and is rare state for the oil market in recent years.

"It's gonna get worse. You have (Norwegian state oil company) Statoil (the world's second largest oil exporter) and the Saudis putting oil into storage, so I look for the contango to be about 10-20 cents, whatever it costs to store it," said an oil trader for a major oil company.
The contango on Wednesday was about seven cents.
The bearish tone in gasoline prices, at a time when a seasonal rally is usally expected, played into current bearish sentiment, traders said.

"With the turn to $6 crude-gasoline (premiums), you'll start seeing sufficient numbers to attract imports to (the U.S. Northeast). I expect to see contango the rest of the year," said another Texas oil trader.

U.S. Gulf refiners returning plants from maintenance will have less impetus to buy domestic barrels due to the cheapness of foreign crude -- especially from the North Sea Brent, West African, Latin American and Canadian supplies.
Statoil was heard offering Norwegian Oseberg and Gullfaks around May WTI minus $1.00 and minus 90 cents, respectively, for end-April or early May arrival.
Wet Brent was sold near a $1.00 discount to May paper Brent in London for April 8-10 loading.
Traders also hummed with talk British Petroleum was amassing Brent for trans-Atlantic shipment, accumulating as much as 10 April Brent cargoes.
"There seems to even be a little bit of a panic to the selling today in the domestics, because of the foreigns," said a trader.
Differentials for Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James dipped to a more than 50 cents discount to WTI markers, from minus 35 cents on Tuesday, with slips also seen in other sweet and sour barrels.
O'Grady said he was not shocked by crude selling, but more interested in what he termed a "mysterious" dip in gasoline prices.
"We are into the driving season. It looks like funds chucked out positions in crude and the gasoline," he said.
--New York Energy Desk, ((+1 212 859 1828))
